reading.body:
Hurricane Electric's Fremont 2 facility holds 3,000 cabinets across 200,000 square feet, making it a major colocation hub in the Bay Area despite publishing no power consumption figures.

The facility is one of three that Hurricane Electric operates in Northern California. Hurricane Electric functions as both an internet service provider and network backbone operator, roles that typically require dense interconnection infrastructure. Colocation facilities like this one lease cabinet space to multiple tenants, which means power demand can vary widely depending on occupancy and customer workloads. The lack of published megawatt capacity makes it impossible to assess how much electricity this facility actually draws or how much headroom it has for AI workload growth.

The 200,000 square foot building with 3,000 cabinets suggests moderate density by data center standards. Without power figures, the data cannot establish whether this facility is a binding constraint on Bay Area compute availability or simply a regional node in a larger network. The facility's colocation model means it serves many operators rather than any single one, which shapes its role in the AI supply chain differently than a hyperscaler's owned-and-operated data center would.
